opus-5.5.text:
I think it really comes down to the fact that simulation is a deep technical discipline in its own right. From the outside it looks like a supporting tool. You render a scene, drop a robot in, and let it practice. But once you try to build simulation that's actually useful for training embodied models, you run into a long list of hard problems.

First, there's physics fidelity. Rigid-body dynamics is relatively mature, but robots in the real world deal with contact-rich manipulation: grasping deformable objects, cloth, liquids, cables, friction that changes with materials. Getting contact and deformation right, and stable enough to run at scale, takes years of accumulated engineering. It's not something a team can hack together in a few months alongside building a robot and a foundation model.

Second, there's content and assets. A simulator is only as good as the worlds you put into it. You need large numbers of diverse, physically accurate objects and scenes: kitchens, warehouses, homes, each with correct geometry, materials, articulation and mass properties. Producing that at scale is basically its own industry. It looks a lot more like a game or film pipeline than robotics research.

Third, there's the sim-to-real gap. The real value isn't a pretty simulation. It's whether policies trained there transfer to physical hardware. Closing that gap requires systematic work on sensor modeling, domain randomization and calibration against real data. That work compounds across many customers and many robot types, which a specialist can amortize but a single robot company can't.

And then there's the strategic question of focus. Embodied-intelligence companies are already fighting on several fronts at once: hardware, data collection, model training, deployment, commercialization. Their scarcest resource is talent and time. If they spend a big chunk of their best engineers rebuilding a physics engine and asset pipeline, that's attention taken away from what actually differentiates them, which is the model and the product.

So it's a familiar pattern from other industries. Early on, everyone builds everything themselves because nothing exists. As the field matures, the infrastructure layers split off and specialize. Chip companies stopped running their own fabs, and app developers stopped running their own servers. I think simulation for embodied AI is going through that same transition right now. The companies that turn to specialists aren't giving up capability. They're recognizing that a shared, continuously improving infrastructure layer moves faster than something each of them maintains alone.

r001.rationale: The response says simulation takes years of engineering and would consume a company’s best engineers, but it does not clearly state that integrating the work requires a critical mass of top-quality talent within one company.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I think it comes down to a very simple calculation that every embodied-intelligence founder makes, usually within the first six months.

When you start a robotics company, your scarce resource isn't money, it's attention. You have maybe a dozen people who really understand the problem you're trying to solve, and every one of them you put on building a simulator is one you're not putting on the actual robot, the actual policy, the actual customer. And simulation looks deceptively easy from the outside. You think, we'll take an open-source physics engine, wrap it, add some assets, done. Then you discover that contact dynamics for a dexterous hand are a research problem in themselves. That rendering realistic enough to transfer to a real camera is its own discipline. That building a pipeline to generate thousands of varied scenes with correct physical properties, not just pretty ones, requires people who have done this before and failed a few times.

So what actually happens is companies build a version 0.5 internally, it gets them to a demo, and then they hit a wall. The sim-to-real gap is too large, or the simulator is too slow to generate the data volumes they need, or the one engineer who understood it leaves. And at that point they look around and realize a specialist has already solved eighty percent of their problem, and more importantly, has solved it for ten other companies, so the remaining twenty percent is being iterated on far faster than they could manage alone.

There's also a data flywheel argument. A simulation company that serves many robot developers sees many more failure modes. Every time a customer tells us the gripper slipping on a deformable object doesn't match reality, that fix benefits everyone. A single company building in-house only sees its own failures.

And I'd add one more thing people underestimate. Simulation is infrastructure, and infrastructure has to be maintained. Engines update, GPU architectures change, asset formats evolve. A robotics company doesn't want to wake up two years in and find that half its engineering team is effectively a tools team. Outsourcing that lets them stay a robotics company.

The honest caveat is that this isn't universal. If your edge is precisely in simulation, if your whole thesis is that you can generate better training data than anyone, then you should build it. But for most teams, the core bet is on the robot and the model, not the simulator. And betting your attention where your thesis lives is just good discipline.

r001.rationale: The response says simulation needs people with specialized experience and competes for a company’s limited attention, but it does not clearly state that integrating the work requires a critical mass of top-quality talent within one company.

astra-6.text:
I think it comes down to focus and the cost of building something well. An embodied-intelligence company needs simulation to develop and test its robots, but building a reliable simulator is a substantial engineering task in its own right. You need physics, sensors, environments, and tools that let you run experiments efficiently. And you have to keep checking whether what happens in simulation corresponds to what happens on the real robot.

A specialist simulation company can spread that investment across multiple customers. For a robotics team, working with one can mean getting useful infrastructure sooner and putting more effort into the robot’s capabilities.

But I wouldn’t frame it as outsourcing everything. The robotics company still needs to understand its own tasks, supply real-world measurements, and judge whether the simulation is accurate enough for a particular use. You can buy the platform; you still have to establish that it helps you build a better robot.

r001.rationale: The response describes simulation as a substantial engineering task and says specialists can spread the investment across customers, but it does not say that building the capability requires a critical mass of top-quality talent within one company to integrate the work.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the core reason is that building a simulator and building a simulator that actually helps train robots are two very different things.

You can get a basic environment running relatively quickly. But making the physics reliable, modeling sensors and contact, generating diverse scenarios, and running everything efficiently at scale takes sustained investment. And then you have to check whether what the robot learns in simulation transfers to the real world. A simulation can look convincing and still teach the wrong behavior.

For an embodied-intelligence company, the question is where to put scarce engineering resources. Its main focus is usually the robot, the model, and the application. A specialist simulation company can spread the cost of developing that infrastructure across multiple customers.

That doesn’t mean the robot company should outsource all its simulation expertise. It still needs to define the tasks, collect real-world measurements, and judge whether the simulator is useful. The strongest arrangement is often to use a specialist platform while keeping that validation loop in-house.

r001.rationale: The response says simulator development takes sustained investment and lists technical challenges, but it does not explain that success requires a critical mass of top-quality talent within one company to integrate the work.
